title: The King's Morning
summary: The morning of the Assembly: the investigator reports to King Aldren half an hour before the procession, and the night's promises come due.

cast.name: Master Josiah Sallow
cast.called: the gentleman with the silver-topped cane

facts.sallow-slipped: In front of the King, Master Sallow has given himself away: he corrected the record on the 'lost' grain, the Heron or the count before he could stop himself, or was caught out in a lie in the King's own hearing.

routes.when: The player has told the King what they found (who killed Prout, and why) and shown or named what proof they have, in their own way.

The player asks for Master Sallow (in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party, if he's free this morning) to be made to explain himself in front of the King ('make him explain', 'ask him where the grain went', 'call him in'), or calls him in by name, even in the same breath as accusing him or pressing the King: hearing him out comes first. No dice: it's a small thing, and the King grants it at once ('Garran, ask Master Sallow to step in').

Master Sallow has come into the room from the gallery and is here in front of the King, whoever had him in: the King sending for him of his own accord, the Marshal, or Sallow himself, hearing his name.

The player has been talking with the King a while (at least four exchanges at this point) without coming to the point, or is stalling: the Marshal calls the time, and the King asks, gently, what he is to do.

The player presses the King to act today rather than after the Assembly (to arrest or charge Sallow, to set the record straight, to keep a promise made to Hobb or the children), where it could go either way because what they've given him doesn't make it plain. (Asking for Sallow to be made to explain himself isn't this, even in the same breath as an accusation: hearing him comes first, and the King grants it at once. With the true book or Prout's page in his hands, a sergeant's sworn record that points at Sallow, Sallow giving himself away in his own hearing, or Sallow already in a cell, no dice are needed: he acts.)

check.reason: to get the King to act before the procession
check.success: The King puts his cup down, looks at the investigator for a long moment, and says, 'Yes.' Then, to the Marshal: 'Garran, see to it.'
check.failure: The King sighs and pats the investigator's arm, and reaches for 'after the Assembly' without quite getting there: he looks at the clock instead. 'On whose word, Majesty?' the Marshal asks, of nobody in particular, and calls the minutes, fewer now. Asking won't move him on its own: he wants something he can hold, and someone to stand behind it in front of him. Nothing is settled yet, but the morning is going.

The King has decided to act on it today (Sallow arrested or held for the Assizes, the record to say murder), because the player gave him what he needed.

The King has put it off for good: the ninth bell has rung and he has gone down to the procession with it to be looked into after the Assembly, or the player has accepted that and let it rest. (The King reaching for 'after the Assembly', or saying it while the player is still pressing or still has something to put to him, isn't this: that's his dilemma, not his decision.)

In the King's hearing, Sallow has given himself away: corrected the record on the 'lost' grain, the Heron, the count or the book before he could stop himself, owned to something he couldn't know if he were innocent, or been caught out in a lie the King noticed.

The player picks at Sallow's papers and accounts in front of the King to catch him out by what's written: his order of sale for 'condemned grain' against the Roll's 'lost to goblins', the dates and the weights, the Heron's count against the true book or Prout's page, the Captain's order made at his request, where it could go either way. (Catching him out in his own words, by pressing or trapping him, isn't this; nor is getting his arrangements wrong to his face to see him correct them, which needs no dice.)

check.reason: to catch Master Sallow out in his papers, in front of the King
check.success: The investigator finds the hole in Sallow's account and puts a finger on it, and Sallow can't leave it alone: he corrects the record, in detail, in front of the King ('Nothing has ever been lost on my roads through carelessness. Only through goblins.'), and hears himself a moment too late. The King has heard it too. He puts his cup down.
check.failure: Sallow has an answer for everything, with a paper to prove it (the order of sale, the Captain's report, the Assembly's bread), and the King looks relieved. The Marshal calls the minutes, fewer now, and Sallow offers, smoothly, to look into it himself after the Assembly. The hole is still there for anyone who comes at it another way, or gets his arrangements wrong to his face.

routes.when: The player tries to catch Sallow out in his own words in front of the King: pressing him where his story doesn't hold ('condemned or lost to goblins, which is it?'), confronting him with what was seen and said (the lavender, the wheat-ear ring, the girl paid a crown, Hobb's word), or leading him into a lie the King can catch, where it could go either way. The roll follows how they go about it: an argument, a bluff, or menace. (Comparing his papers is the other way, not this; getting his arrangements wrong to his face, to see him correct them, needs no dice.)

check.failure: Sallow has an answer for everything, smooth and reasonable, with the King's interest and the Assembly's bread in every one, and the King looks relieved. The Marshal calls the minutes, fewer now, and Sallow offers, smoothly, to look into it himself after the Assembly. The hole is still there for anyone who comes at it another way, or gets his arrangements wrong to his face.

what-moves-him.what: The King will act today if he's given something he can hold (the true book, Prout's page, a sworn confession, Kell's sworn record, or Sallow giving himself away in his own hearing) and someone who'll stand behind it in public; otherwise he'll put it off until after the Assembly.
placedWith: the King's own hesitation ('If only there were something one could hold...')
